traveler: Plinio el Viejo (Gaius Plinius Secundus, Pliny the Elder)
title: The Lake, the Rhine, and the Cloud Like a Pine: the Admiral Who Wrote Down the World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Novum Comum and the Schools of Rome

stops.name: Novum Comum, the birth on Lake Larius
stops.date_confidence: disputed: Wikipedia and most handbooks give AD 23, Livius.org gives AD 24, and neither rests on a dated document; both are back-calculations from the age at death. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 1 January.
stops.campa: A son is born to an equestrian family at Novum Comum, on the western arm of Lake Larius, under Tiberius. The family holds property around the water and stands high enough in the town that both its Plinys will be remembered there as native sons. The names given for the father and mother, Gaius Plinius Celer and Marcella, come from one fragmentary and disputed inscription and from no literary source at all; the atlas records them as tradition and not as fact. He is Gaius Plinius Secundus, and the lake will outlast every book he writes but one.
stops.quote: man alone, poore wretch, she hath laid all naked upon the bare earth, even on his birth-day, to cry and wraule presently from the very first houre that he is borne into this world.
stops.quote_source: Naturalis Historia VII, proem, trans. Philemon Holland (1601)
suggested_refs: The Roman forum area of Novum Comum, under the streets of modern Como

stops.name: Rome, the schools and the courts of two emperors
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the years between roughly AD 35 and the first military posting are close to blank. The teachers are attested; no source names a school, a street, or a year.
stops.campa: He is sent to Rome for the education an equestrian family of provincial standing owes its son. He hears the orator Marcus Servilius Nonianus speak, and he studies under Publius Pomponius Secundus, tragedian and grammarian, whose life he will one day write in two books. The teachers are named in the record and the classroom is not. Livius.org places him near the courts of Caligula and Claudius in these years, which is likely for a young man of his rank and is stated outright nowhere.
suggested_refs: The rhetorical schools of the Forum district, location unrecorded
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5 (the Life of Pomponius Secundus)

stops.name: Castra Vetera, praefectus cohortis under Corbulo
stops.date_confidence: the departure for the Rhine is dated 45 by Livius.org and 46 by Wikipedia, an unresolved disagreement; the Vetera posting around 47 is reconstruction. The pin is the fortress of Vetera I on the Fuerstenberg near Birten, not the modern town of Xanten.
stops.campa: He crosses the Alps as a junior officer in his early twenties and reports to Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo on the lower Rhine. As praefectus cohortis he serves in the campaign against the Chauci and the Frisians, in a province where the frontier is a river and the enemy stands on both banks of it. The fortress of Vetera sits on high ground above the water, a legionary town of timber and ditch. Claudius will recall Corbulo before the war is finished; the young officer stays, and learns the country he will spend twenty books describing.
suggested_refs: Vetera I on the Fuerstenberg near Birten, the double legionary fortress of the lower Rhine
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pliny the Elder', citing Naturalis Historia and Tacitus

stops.name: Fossa Corbulonis, the canal between the rivers
stops.date_confidence: attested to Corbulo's command in AD 47; the season of Pliny's part in it is not recorded. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Forbidden a war, Corbulo sets the legions to digging. A canal is cut between the Meuse and the Rhine so that supply ships need never risk the open North Sea, and Pliny is there for the work. He writes of this coast afterwards with the flatness of a man reporting what he has walked on: the tides, the peat, the people who live on raised mounds and burn earth for fuel because they have no wood. Tacitus records the digging of the canal. Pliny records the ground it was cut through.
suggested_refs: The Fossa Corbulonis, traced by excavation near Forum Hadriani at Voorburg

stops.name: Flevum, the coast of the Chauci
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source names the fort of his posting, and Flevum stands here only as the best-attested Roman base in the theatre of these operations. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: North of the Rhine mouth the fleet works along a coast of mud and shifting islands against the Chauci. No ancient text names the fort Pliny is stationed at, and Flevum is the likeliest base rather than a recorded one. The people of these flats live, he writes later, without cattle and without trees, catching fish in nets of reed and drinking rainwater caught in ditches; he calls them wretched, and notes that they call themselves free, and that Rome conquering them would be doing them no favour.
suggested_refs: The Roman fort at Velsen, identified with Flevum, on the Frisian shore
sources: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 16.2-4 (the coastal Chauci)

stops.name: Germania, the dream of Drusus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Epistulae 3.5.4 says only 'cum in Germania militaret': it names no fortress, no season, no year, and no rank. Vetera is a likely garrison and nothing more, and the date is a placeholder within the German service.
stops.campa: Sleeping under the German winter, he sees the shape of Nero Claudius Drusus standing over him, dead sixty years, asking to be rescued from the injury of being forgotten. He wakes and begins the Bella Germaniae, twenty books on every war Rome has fought against the Germanic peoples. He will finish it and it will vanish entirely. His nephew tells the story sixty years later in a letter about his uncle's writing habits, and that letter is the only account of why the books were begun and the only reason anyone knows they existed.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5.4, the sole source for the dream and for the twenty lost books
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5.4 (Latin and Firth translation at attalus.org/old/pliny3.html)

stops.name: Mogontiacum, tribune under his old teacher
stops.date_confidence: around 50 to 51. No ancient text names his post; the Mainz garrison is modern reconstruction, and the pin is the fortress on the Kaestrich plateau rather than the riverside town.
stops.campa: Promoted military tribune, he serves in Germania Superior under Publius Pomponius Secundus, the man who taught him grammar and tragedy in Rome twenty years earlier. The campaign runs against the Chatti; the fortress on the plateau above the Rhine is the likely garrison, though no text says so. He visits the hot springs of the Mattiaci and goes looking for the reputed sources of the Danube, which he will report as travelers report such things, at one remove and with the doubt left in. The teacher commands; the pupil takes notes.
suggested_refs: The legionary fortress of Mogontiacum on the Kaestrich, Mainz
The thermal springs of Aquae Mattiacae at Wiesbaden

stops.name: Lacus Fucinus, the sea-battle on the lake
stops.date_confidence: the naumachia is firmly dated to AD 52. Why Pliny is in Italy in the middle of the German service, no source explains. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Claudius means to drain the Fucine lake and stages a naval battle on it first, thousands of condemned men in warships fighting for an emperor's afternoon. Pliny is in the crowd. What he keeps of it is a detail of dress: Agrippina the Younger watching in a military cloak woven throughout of gold thread, which he reports on his own authority, as a man who saw it. He is a soldier home from the Rhine, standing in a crowd of civilians. The condemned men get no description from him. The cloak does.
suggested_refs: The drained bed of Lacus Fucinus and the outlet tunnel of Claudius near Avezzano

stops.name: Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, praefectus alae
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the cavalry command is attested, the Cologne connection is inference from the governor's seat rather than a recorded posting. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Back on the lower Rhine he commands an ala, a cavalry wing of some four hundred and eighty horse. Cologne is the governor's seat and his likely point of contact with provincial command, even if his own troopers are quartered elsewhere; the sources give the rank and not the address. In these years he writes De Jaculatione Equestri, on throwing the javelin from horseback, a manual by a serving officer for serving officers. It is lost, like everything he writes before the last book.
suggested_refs: The praetorium of Germania Inferior under Cologne's town hall square
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5 (the catalogue of works)

stops.name: Castra Vetera, the harness disc with his name
stops.date_confidence: his last commander, Pompeius Paullinus, governs around 55 to 58. The phalera itself is undated and is suggestive rather than probative: harness travels and names repeat.
stops.campa: A phalera, a decorated disc from a set of harness, comes out of the ground at Vetera with his name on it. It is suggestive and it proves nothing. His last commander in Germany is Pompeius Paullinus, whom he names himself in the thirty-third book while noting that the man carried twelve thousand pounds of embossed silver plate on campaign against the Germans, and fought them with it in his baggage. Some thirteen years on the frontier end here, and he goes home to Italy at thirty-six.
suggested_refs: The inscribed phalera from Castra Vetera bearing the name of Plinius

stops.name: Rome, the return and the twenty books
stops.date_confidence: Livius.org dates the return to 59, at thirty-six; the Bella Germaniae and the Life of Pomponius Secundus are dated around 58. Whether the twenty books were finished on the Rhine or after the homecoming, no source states.
stops.campa: He comes back to Italy with the German wars written out: twenty books of history, and two more on the life of the teacher who commanded him. Neither survives. What survives is the fact that a cavalry officer spent his campaigns compiling, and that Tacitus, working the same ground two generations later, will use him for it. The Rome he returns to is Nero's. He is a friend of Vespasian, a man of no faction, and he has just published a history of victories won under a dynasty that is running out.
suggested_refs: The lost Bella Germaniae in twenty books, used by Tacitus and gone by the Middle Ages

stops.name: Rome, the safe books
stops.date_confidence: the works are attested by Epistulae 3.5; the placement within Nero's reign is approximate and the year is a convenience.
stops.campa: He keeps away from office and writes on subjects that cannot be read as comment. Three books on training an orator, starting from the exercises of childhood; eight books on the ambiguities of Latin usage, undertaken, his nephew says, because grammar was the one field in which a man under Nero could not be accused of meaning something. Both are lost. The nephew is explicit that the choice was self-protection rather than taste, and offers no other reason for a decade of a working man's silence.
stops.quote: If you were a student, you could not waste your hours like that
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: Studiosus in three books and Dubii Sermonis in eight, both lost

stops.name: Rome, the Golden House over the burned city
stops.date_confidence: the fire is dated July 64. That Pliny witnessed it is attested nowhere and is not claimed here; his sight of the colossus is his own statement, and undated.
stops.campa: Nero's Golden House goes up over the ground the fire cleared, a palace with a lake inside it and a bronze colossus of the emperor at the entrance, a hundred and twenty feet of Zenodorus's work. Pliny writes about it with contempt and with measurements, and says of the statue that he saw it himself. Whether he was in the city on the nights the fire burned, no source says and he never claims. He is past forty and has published nothing that anyone will be reading in a hundred years.
stops.quote: it is ridiculous to suppose, that the great head of all things, whatever it be, pays any regard to human affairs
stops.quote_source: Naturalis Historia II.5, trans. Bostock and Riley (1855)
suggested_refs: The Colle Oppio wing of the Domus Aurea and the base of the Colossus of Nero
sources: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 34.45-46 and 36.111

stops.name: Ostia, the embarkation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout: no text places Pliny at Ostia on any day. Procurators ordinarily sailed from here, and that is the whole of the evidence.
stops.campa: Vespasian comes out of the civil wars with the throne, and the friend from the Rhine is put back to work. What follows is four provinces in six years, or three, or two: the sequence is Ronald Syme's reconstruction from regional detail in the Natural History and not a record of anything. No document places Pliny in this harbour. Procurators sail from Ostia, and so the atlas sets him here at the head of a decade whose itinerary is entirely inferred, and says plainly that it is inferring.
suggested_refs: The Claudian and Trajanic harbour basins at Portus, beside Ostia
sources: General practice of the cursus publicus; no direct attestation for Pliny
Ronald Syme, 'Pliny the Procurator', HSCP 73 (1969), cited at second hand

stops.name: Narbo Martius, the proposed Gallic post
stops.date_confidence: disputed. Syme proposes Narbonensis around 70; other reconstructions put him in Africa in the same years, and the two compete rather than combine. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: A procuratorship in Gallia Narbonensis is proposed for these years on the strength of what he knows about the province: its vines, its lagoons, its salt. The argument is that a man writes this way about a country he has administered. The counter-argument is that he writes this way about countries he never saw, because he read four hundred authors and took notes on all of them. Nothing at Narbonne records his name. The post exists in modern scholarship and in no ancient sentence.
suggested_refs: The Capitolium and forum of Narbo Martius, capital of Gallia Narbonensis
sources: Ronald Syme, 'Pliny the Procurator', HSCP 73 (1969), cited at second hand

stops.name: Carthage, the Byrsa hill
stops.date_confidence: disputed and reconstructed. No ancient source states that Pliny held office in Africa; it is inference from books 5 and 8 of the Natural History, competing with the Narbonensis proposal for the same years.
stops.campa: An African procuratorship is inferred from how much of the province sits in his books: the grain, the lions, the fig from Carthage that Cato is said to have shaken out onto the floor of the Senate to argue for a war. He gives a Greek proverb about the place, that Africa always brings forth something new and strange, and it outlives him by two thousand years in a shorter Latin form he never wrote. No ancient source puts him in office here. It is Syme's inference and the atlas flags it as one.
stops.quote: That Africke evermore bringeth forth some new and strange thing or other.
stops.quote_source: Naturalis Historia VIII.16, trans. Philemon Holland (1601)
suggested_refs: The Byrsa hill at Carthage, seat of the proconsular administration
sources: Ronald Syme, 'Pliny the Procurator', cited at second hand
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia books 5 and 8

stops.name: Tacape, the timed water of the oasis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the passage is vivid enough that many read it as eyewitness, and he never says he was there. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: At the oasis on the edge of the Syrtis a single spring is divided among the growers by the hour, each man's share released to him at a set time and cut off at a set time. Under the palms grow olives, under the olives figs, under the figs pomegranates, under those vines, and under the vines grain and then pulses and then garden greens, all in one soil in one year. He sets the arrangement down step by step. Whether he stood in that shade or read about it, the text does not say.
suggested_refs: The palm oasis and spring of Tacape, modern Gabes

stops.name: Tarraco, procurator of Hispania
stops.date_confidence: the best attested of the postings, on Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5.17. The year is approximate. Contrary to some summaries, the Natural History nowhere states that he held the office.
stops.campa: This is the one province the record actually gives him. His nephew writes that while his uncle was procurator in Spain, Larcius Licinius offered him four hundred thousand sesterces for the notebooks, a hundred and sixty volumes written in the smallest of hands on both sides of the sheet, and that he refused. The story is usually told backwards, with Pliny as the buyer and the scholar as the seller. He is the seller who would not sell. He leaves Spain carrying the notes that will become the thirty-seven books.
suggested_refs: The provincial forum of Tarraco, seat of the procurator of Hispania Citerior

stops.name: Las Medulas, the ruin of the mountains
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the passage is often read as direct inspection during the Spanish procuratorship, and he does not say he was there. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: In the gold country of the northwest, mountains are taken apart with water. Miners cut galleries through the rock by lamplight for months on end without seeing daylight, then the props are drawn and the hillside comes down with a crash no human mind could conceive, and the reservoirs above are opened onto the wreck to wash the gold out of it. Pliny sets out the method stage by stage, including what the watchmen shout when the mountain goes. He calls it a victory over nature. He does not call it a good one.
suggested_refs: The collapsed red faces of Las Medulas and the surviving Roman water channels

stops.name: Augusta Treverorum, the winter that split the vines
stops.date_confidence: disputed and reconstructed: a Belgica procuratorship is proposed from Naturalis Historia 17.3, a frost among the Treveri read as local and immediate. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: A fourth procuratorship, in Gallia Belgica, rests on one sentence about weather: a cold so hard in the country of the Treveri that the bark split away from the vines. Scholars read the detail as the note of a man standing in the vineyard. It could as easily be a report forwarded to Rome and copied into a file. Twenty-five years after his first posting he is back on the same rivers, no longer a cavalry officer but a man with a ledger, and the whole evidence for his being there is a frost.
suggested_refs: Augusta Treverorum, provincial capital of Gallia Belgica
sources: Ronald Syme, 'Pliny the Procurator', cited at second hand

segments.name: Vespasian's Rome and the Thirty-Seven Books

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years around 71 to 79 as a habit of life rather than as a dated event; the year here marks the return from the provinces.
stops.campa: He calls on Vespasian while it is still night, because the emperor also works before dawn, and goes from the palace to his official duties and from those to his desk. In summer he eats light, then sleeps in the sun with a book read aloud beside him and a secretary taking down whatever he marks. In the bath, being scraped and dried, he is still dictating. On the road he keeps a shorthand writer at his elbow with a glove on the man's hand against the cold, and reproaches his nephew for walking, because those hours could have been used.
stops.quote: He could sleep at call, and it would come upon him and leave him in the middle of his work
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: The Flavian imperial residence on the Palatine, where he made his pre-dawn calls

stops.name: Rome, the Temple of Peace
stops.date_confidence: the temple is dedicated in 75; his use of its contents is undated and is placed here for the dedication year. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Vespasian fills the Temple of Peace with the art of the world, some of it Nero's and some of it Jerusalem's, and Pliny walks through it taking notes for the books on painting and bronze and marble. He is honest about the limits: much of what he reports on where the famous works of Rome now stand comes out of earlier books and not out of his own eyes, and he says so in the text. The catalogue of Greek art that survives only through him is assembled here, inside a building raised on the spoils of a war he did not fight.
stops.quote: there never was a book so bad that it was not good in some passage or another
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 3.5, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: The Templum Pacis of Vespasian and its displayed Greek masterworks
sources: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 34.84 and 36.27

stops.name: Rome, thirty-seven books for Titus
stops.date_confidence: attested by the dedication, which names Titus's sixth consulship, AD 77. Composition is thought to begin after 70, which is inference. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He publishes the Naturalis Historia and dedicates it to Titus: thirty-seven books, twenty thousand facts worth knowing, gathered out of a hundred authors and two thousand volumes, with a summary at the front so that an emperor need not read the whole of it. Nobody before him has tried to write down the world. On the nature of God he declines the comfort his readers expect, and says the only certainty the question yields is that there is no certainty in it at all.
stops.quote: among all of them this alone is certain, that there is nothing certain
stops.quote_source: Naturalis Historia II.5, trans. Bostock and Riley (1855)
suggested_refs: The preface of the Naturalis Historia, addressed to Titus in his sixth consulship
sources: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia, preface

stops.name: Rome, nature as parent and as stepmother
stops.date_confidence: the passage is undated within the work and is placed here at publication. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The seventh book opens on man and cannot decide what nature is to him. Every other animal she clothes or arms or shells; man alone she lays down naked on the bare ground on the day he is born, to cry from his first hour. It is hard to judge, he writes, whether in doing that she played the kind mother or the hard and cruel stepmother. An admiral of the fleet is writing about infants. Two years later he will die at the foot of a mountain in the dark, on the terms he has just written down.
stops.quote: In so much, as it is hard to iudge, whether in so doing, she hath done the part of a kind mother, or a hard and cruell step-dame.
stops.quote_source: Naturalis Historia VII, proem, trans. Philemon Holland (1601)
suggested_refs: The proem to Book VII, the most quoted passage of the Natural History
sources: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia VII, proem (Holland 1601, penelope.uchicago.edu)

stops.name: Misenum, praefectus classis
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is dated around 77 to 79. Vespasian, not Titus, gave him the fleet; Titus is the dedicatee of the book and nothing more. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Vespasian gives him the largest naval command in the empire: the fleet at Misenum, at the tip of the Bay of Naples, watered by a cistern cut into the hill. He is in his mid-fifties and lives in the house by the harbour with his widowed sister Plinia and her son, a boy of seventeen who reads Livy and makes extracts. Cicero came home through Puteoli a mile up this coast a hundred and fifty years before; Virgil lies buried on the Posillipo road; the Aeneid buries Aeneas's trumpeter Misenus at the cape that gives the base its name.
suggested_refs: The Piscina Mirabilis, the great cistern of the Misenum fleet

stops.name: Baiae, the oyster beds
stops.date_confidence: his contempt for the resort is attested in the ninth book; no dated visit is recorded. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Three miles along the shore, Rome takes its pleasure. Baiae is villas built out over the water, heated pools, and the oyster beds of the Lucrine lake, which one Sergius Orata invented for profit and which Pliny records as an invention of the same order as the aqueducts and worse in its effects. He lives beside the most expensive coast in the world and writes about it the way a quartermaster writes about waste. The bay he despises is the bay he will not leave.
suggested_refs: The submerged villas of Baiae and the Lucrine oyster beds

stops.name: Misenum, the cloud like a pine
stops.date_confidence: the traditional date. A charcoal inscription found at Pompeii in 2018 and dated to mid-October has reopened the case for an autumn eruption; the dispute is live and is not resolved here. Vespasian has been dead two months, not the four often printed.
stops.campa: About the seventh hour his sister comes to tell him that a cloud of unusual size and shape is standing over the bay. He is lying down with his books after a cold bath and a light lunch. He calls for his shoes and climbs to the highest ground in the house to look. The cloud rises on a long trunk and spreads at the top into branches, white in places and elsewhere blotched and dirty with the earth and ash it is carrying, and from Misenum it is not yet certain which mountain it is coming out of.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16, the founding description of a Plinian column
sources: Parco Archeologico di Pompei, 2018 charcoal graffito dating

stops.name: Capo Miseno, the light vessel ordered
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed as above. The order of events here follows Epistulae 6.16.7-9 and is routinely collapsed in retellings, which merge the observation boat and the rescue fleet into one command.
stops.campa: He judges it worth seeing close and orders a fast Liburnian galley made ready, and offers his nephew the place if he wants it. The boy says he would rather keep working, and is left with his Livy. What is being launched at this moment is a scientific errand and nothing else: one light boat, one man who wants a better view of a thing nobody has described. The fleet is still at anchor. The change comes within the next few minutes, and it comes in a note carried by a slave.
suggested_refs: The promontory of Capo Miseno, the lookout above the fleet anchorage

stops.name: Porto Miseno, the message from Rectina
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed. Some manuscripts and editors read the name as a place, Retina, rather than as a woman, Rectina; the reading is unsettled and is left open.
stops.campa: A note reaches him from Rectina, wife of Tascius, whose house stands at the foot of the mountain and who has no way out except by sea. He changes the order. The quadriremes go down the slipways, the whole weight of the fleet, and he boards himself to bring off not one household but as many people as that shore holds. He is hurrying, his nephew writes, to the place from which everyone else is running, holding the helm straight at the thing and calling out what he sees to be written down as he goes.
suggested_refs: The harbour basin of Portus Misenus, home of the praetorian fleet

stops.name: Off Herculaneum, the stone on the decks
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed.
stops.campa: Ash falls on the ships, hotter and thicker as they close, then pumice, then blackened stones burnt and cracked by fire. The sea shoals where the mountain has thrown its debris into it, and the shore is blocked by what has come down off the slope. The helmsman says turn back. Pliny says fortune favours the bold and gives the course for Pomponianus at Stabiae. He is in his mid-fifties, heavy, short of breath at the best of times, and he is dictating observations while it happens.
stops.quote: Fortune favours the bold; try to reach Pomponianus.
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: The buried Roman shoreline of Herculaneum, with the boat chambers and their skeletons

stops.name: The shore below the mountain, the villa unreached
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed. The villa is unlocated and even the name is a textual variant; the pin marks the stretch of shore and not a building.
stops.campa: The house that called him is somewhere along this shore under the mountain, and he never reaches it. The wind that carries him down the bay is the wind that will not let him in. Somewhere close by, going under in the same hours, is the villa whose library of carbonized rolls will come out of the ground seventeen centuries later, the one a modern reconstruction wants to make the school where Virgil studied Epicurus under Siro. Rectina is not heard of again in any source, and nobody knows whether she got off.
suggested_refs: The Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, buried by the same fall
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16.8, with the manuscript variant Retina

stops.name: Stabiae, the villa of Pomponianus
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed.
stops.campa: He lands at Stabiae, where Pomponianus has his baggage already in the boats and is waiting only for the wind to turn. Pliny embraces him, tells him to take heart, and to prove there is nothing to be afraid of asks to be taken to the bath. Bathed, he lies down and dines, and he is cheerful, or gives a good imitation of cheerfulness, which his nephew notes is just as impressive. Across the water, broad sheets of flame are standing up off Vesuvius and lighting the whole slope.
suggested_refs: The cliff-top villas of Stabiae above the Sarno plain

stops.name: Stabiae, the night in the courtyard
stops.date_confidence: the night of 24 to 25 August by the traditional dating, disputed as above.
stops.campa: He goes to bed and sleeps, and the men at his door hear him snoring, because he is heavy and his breathing is loud. The courtyard outside fills with ash and pumice until the door will soon not open, and they wake him. The house rocks with shocks as though it were coming off its foundations; outside, stones are falling out of the dark. They argue it out and choose the open air, and tie pillows onto their heads with strips of cloth against what is coming down, and walk out.
suggested_refs: The pillow and cloth of Epistulae 6.16.16, the first recorded volcanic head protection

stops.name: The shore at Stabiae, the death
stops.date_confidence: traditional date, disputed. The cause is contested: thick fumes on the nephew's own inference, apoplexy or heart failure per Jacob Bigelow in 1859, and Suetonius transmits a rumour that Pliny asked a slave to kill him.
stops.campa: The sea is still too wild to launch. He lies down on a sailcloth spread for him, asks twice for cold water and drinks it. Flames come on with a smell of sulphur and the others run; he stands up with a slave under each arm and drops at once. His nephew, writing from hearsay a generation later, puts it down to a weak throat and thick air. Suetonius passes on a different story, that he asked to be killed. In 1859 a Boston physician reads the same page and says it was his heart.
stops.quote: Leaning on two slaves, he rose to his feet and immediately fell down again, owing, as I think, to his breathing being obstructed by the thickness of the fumes and congestion of the stomach, that organ being naturally weak and narrow, and subject to inflammation.
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: The ancient beach line at Stabiae, now inland of the modern shore
sources: Suetonius, fragmentary life of Pliny, via later tradition
Jacob Bigelow, 1859 medical analysis, cited at second hand

stops.name: Misenum, the dark across the bay
stops.date_confidence: traditional dating, disputed. Epistulae 6.20 does not synchronise precisely with 6.16, and the hours cannot be matched between the two letters.
stops.campa: Twenty miles west, his sister and his nephew are living the same hours. The sea is sucked back off the beach and left with stranded creatures on it. Then the dark comes over, and the boy writes afterwards that it was not the dark of a moonless night or of cloud, but the dark of a shut room with the lamp put out: women screaming, children calling, men shouting for people they could not see and knowing each other only by voice. He is seventeen, and he is already writing it down.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.20, the second Vesuvius letter

stops.name: The shore at Stabiae, the body
stops.date_confidence: corrected: Epistulae 6.16.20 gives the third day counting inclusively from 24 August, that is 26 August, two days after the death and not the three days often printed. Traditional dating, disputed as above.
stops.campa: The light comes back on the third day counted from the last day he saw, and they find him where he fell, the body whole and unmarked, the clothes as they had been. He looks, his nephew writes, more like a man asleep than a man dead. Nothing is recorded of what was done with him afterwards. There is no tomb, no marker, no ashes anyone has identified, and no ancient source claims there ever was one. The most famous corpse of the eruption is the one nobody buried on the record.
stops.quote: When daylight returned, two days after the last day he had seen, his body was found untouched, uninjured, and covered, dressed just as he had been in life. The corpse suggested a person asleep rather than a dead man.
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16, trans. J. B. Firth (1900)
suggested_refs: The absence of any identified tomb or remains, an unfilled gap in the record

stops.name: Pompeii, the town under the ash
stops.date_confidence: traditional dating, disputed.
stops.campa: Six miles from where he died, a town of some eleven thousand goes under the fall he sailed into, and stays under for sixteen centuries. Goethe and Johann Tischbein walk the half-cleared forum in the spring of 1787 and find the disaster oddly cheerful. Edward Bulwer-Lytton comes in 1833, writes The Last Days of Pompeii, and hands the eruption to the English-reading world as a novel with a blind flower girl in it. Both of them are walking on the ground Pliny was trying to reach.
suggested_refs: The forum of Pompeii as it stood half-excavated in 1787

stops.name: Novum Comum, the will and the nephew's name
stops.date_confidence: the adoption is epigraphic, CIL V 5262; the benefactions are spread across the nephew's later life and are dated here only at the head of the sequence. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The will makes the nephew heir on condition that he take the name, and Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus enters the record as a Plinius Secundus. In time he gives the lake town a library, a school, and a fund to feed and educate freeborn children, and the family's money goes back into the place the family came out of. The inscription recording the adoption survives. The uncle's hundred and sixty notebooks, refused to Larcius Licinius for four hundred thousand sesterces, do not.
suggested_refs: CIL V 5262, the Comum inscription naming the younger Pliny as adopted son

stops.name: Rome, the letter to Tacitus
stops.date_confidence: around 106, roughly twenty-seven years after the eruption; the exact year is not fixed. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Tacitus writes asking for an account of the death, for the Histories. The nephew is in his forties now and answers with two letters: one for the uncle at Stabiae, one for himself and his mother at Misenum. He says at the outset that he will be glad if the death gets an undying fame out of the telling. Tacitus's own version is lost with that part of the Histories. What survives of the best documented death in the ancient world is the letter written to supply somebody else's book.
suggested_refs: Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20, written for a lost passage of Tacitus's Histories

stops.name: York, the Leiden Pliny
stops.date_confidence: eighth or ninth century; the manuscript is not precisely dated, and the year here is a placeholder. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: No complete ancient copy of the Natural History survives. It comes down through three separate lines: burnt fragments of fifth and sixth century palimpsests, the older manuscripts of the eighth and ninth centuries, and the ninth century copies behind the medieval standard text. One of the oldest is written out in large format in Northumbria in Bede's century and now sits at Leiden. The world's first encyclopaedia reaches the modern world by way of a scriptorium at York.
suggested_refs: The Leiden Pliny, a large-format vetustior produced at York
sources: Manuscript tradition of the Naturalis Historia, modern philological consensus

stops.name: Venice, the editio princeps
stops.date_confidence: 1469 is firm. The printer attribution is contested: generally credited to Johannes de Spira alone, since Wendelin took over the press only after his brother's death in 1470, though both names circulate. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Fourteen years after the Gutenberg Bible, the Natural History is set in type at Venice, one of the earliest classical texts to reach print at all. The press is that of Johannes de Spira; the common attribution to him and his brother Wendelin together cannot stand, because Wendelin does not take the press over until 1470. The text underlying it is imperfect, and no complete critical edition of the Latin exists even now. Three centuries of European natural science get built on that text.
suggested_refs: The 1469 Venice editio princeps of the Naturalis Historia
sources: Printing history of the Naturalis Historia

stops.name: Como, the two statues on the cathedral front
stops.date_confidence: the west front is built between 1457 and 1498; the statues are not separately dated. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Como finishes its cathedral front with a portal flanked by two seated figures, the uncle and the nephew in Renaissance dress, put up by a town that claims them both. It is a Christian church with two pagans on the door, one of whom wrote that a supreme being's interest in human business is a ridiculous thing to suppose. The claim to his birth here rests on the nephew's letters about family property by the lake, which is thin, and which has been good enough for five hundred years.
suggested_refs: The west front of Como Cathedral with its seated Plinys
sources: Como Cathedral facade, west front construction record

stops.name: Torno, the Villa Pliniana
stops.date_confidence: begun 1573 for Giovanni Anguissola, finished 1577. The Plinian association is toponymic and promotional, not an ancient site. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: On the eastern shore of the lake a villa goes up beside an intermittent spring that rises and falls several times a day, the spring the younger Pliny described in a letter and the elder listed among the wonders of water. The house takes their name and has no other connection to them: a sixteenth century property borrowing a first century name because the name carries. Shelley and Rossini will stay in it. The spring keeps its own schedule and owes nothing to either Pliny.
suggested_refs: Villa Pliniana at Torno and its intermittent spring

stops.name: Vesuvius, the crater and the word
stops.date_confidence: the stop is dated to Humboldt's 1805 ascents. The coiner and first scientific use of the term 'Plinian' could not be established from reachable sources and is recorded as an open gap. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Athanasius Kircher has himself lowered into this crater on a rope in 1638 and comes back up with the beginnings of Mundus Subterraneus. Alexander von Humboldt climbs it repeatedly in 1805 taking readings inside an active eruption, with Simon Bolivar beside him by a tradition the atlas flags as unconfirmed. Giordano Bruno grew up under it at Nola; Hannibal wintered under it at Capua. Volcanology names the tall sustained column after a Pliny, but the nephew who described it, not the uncle who sailed in.
suggested_refs: The crater rim of Vesuvius, descended by Kircher in 1638 and measured by Humboldt in 1805
